issues.item: Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
issues.explanation: The profile is not well aligned with the cognitive formulation. The only active edge is Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly arise from the selected appraisals. Overeating and busyness can follow from distressing appraisals, but 'Checking Surroundings' is a threat-monitoring/safety behavior that usually implies an active Threat component or a strong Trigger/Threat linkage, both of which are absent in the formulation and not represented elsewhere in the self-report.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'Fear of Harm' is a global current-danger appraisal that typically pairs with a Threat presentation and supports behaviors like environmental scanning. But Threat is not represented as an active component in the formulation, and the rest of the negative appraisals are more about self-doubt and shattered assumptions. This makes the appraisal/strategy pattern clinically incoherent for the specified edge structure.

vignette:
Harold is a 77-year-old married man who has worked as a delivery driver for most of his adult life, a job he has always taken quiet pride in - the independence of the road, the predictability of routes, the small dignities of showing up on time and doing things right. That sense of reliable order was shattered several months ago when he was assaulted during a late-afternoon delivery in a neighbourhood he had driven through hundreds of times before. A man approached him at the back of his truck, demanded his phone and the cash in his shirt pocket, and when Harold hesitated - not out of defiance but out of sheer disbelief that this was actually happening - he was struck twice across the face and shoved hard against the vehicle's rear door. The whole episode lasted under two minutes. Harold drove the rest of his route in a daze, hands trembling on the wheel, and did not tell his wife what had happened until three days later.

In the weeks that followed, Harold found that the world he thought he understood had quietly ceased to make sense. He had lived nearly eight decades on the assumption that if you kept your head down, worked honestly, and treated people decently, you would be more or less safe - that the social contract, however imperfect, held. The assault had not merely frightened him; it had demolished something foundational. He had come to believe, in a way he could not fully articulate but felt constantly, that his judgement about people and situations could no longer be trusted. Standing at a customer's door, reading someone's expression, deciding whether to linger or move on - these had once been automatic. Now they felt like gambles he was certain to lose. The self-doubt was not abstract. It was in his hands when he reached for a package, in his eyes scanning a driveway, in the half-second pause before he knocked. He was no longer sure he would do the right thing when it mattered, and that uncertainty sat in him like a stone.

What frightened Harold most about the memory itself was the conviction that engaging with it would undo him entirely. He was certain that if he allowed himself to think about the assault - to replay the sound of the impact, the cold metal of the truck door against his back - he would not be able to hold himself together, that something would break that could not be repaired. So he did not let himself go there. He worked longer hours than his body probably warranted for a man his age, filling every available hour with the motion of driving, loading, unloading, checking manifests. Busyness had become a kind of architecture he built around himself each day, and when the routes ended and the quiet came, he ate - more than he needed, more than felt good - because the fullness was something physical to attend to, something that briefly displaced the formless dread. His wife had noticed the weight he was putting on and had gently said something twice; Harold had changed the subject both times.

These strategies - the relentless movement, the overeating, the deliberate suppression of any thought that veered too close to that afternoon - were not arbitrary. They were the direct consequence of what Harold had come to believe about himself and the world. Because he was convinced that thinking about the event would destroy him, he suppressed it. Because he no longer trusted his own responses to be adequate, he kept himself too busy to be tested. The appraisals drove the coping, and the coping, in its way, preserved the appraisals intact - never examined, never challenged, growing heavier with each passing week.

The concrete cost had become impossible to ignore. Harold had begun refusing certain delivery zones - areas that resembled, in some quality of light or street layout, the neighbourhood where the assault occurred. His dispatcher had noticed the pattern and raised it with him directly last week. It was that conversation, more than anything, that brought Harold to seek help. He was not ready to lose the work. Driving was who he was. What he most hoped for, sitting in the intake chair, was some way to feel like himself again on the road - and what he most feared was that the person he had been before that afternoon was simply gone.
